slides.text:
Every function so far took a fixed number of arguments. A **variadic** function takes as many as the caller wants: none, one or fifty. You will declare one, loop over what it receives, and hand it a whole list at once.

The snippet is pseudo code, not Go.
slides.code:
total(1, 2)
total(5, 6, 7, 8)
total()

same function, any number of values

slides.text: Put `...` before the type of the **last** parameter. The caller can then pass any number of values of that type, including none.

Inside the function, the parameter is a **slice**: an ordered list of values of one type. You do not build slices yet. Here you only read one, the way you read a string: `len` counts its values and `range` walks over them.

The snippet is pseudo code.
slides.code:
call(4, 5, 6)   values = 4, 5, 6
call(9)         values = 9
call()          values = nothing

slides.text: Other parameters can come before the variadic one. They are normal parameters, and the variadic one takes whatever is left.

exercises.title: Add any amount of numbers
exercises.guide: Write a function that adds up every number it receives.

chunks.guide: `...int` lets the caller pass any number of ints. Inside, `nums` is a list you walk with `range`, as you did with a string.

notes.text: Zero or more ints may be passed.

chunks.guide: The same function is called with a different number of arguments each time.

exercises.title: Count the arguments
exercises.guide: Return how many strings the caller passed.

chunks.guide: `len` works on the variadic parameter: it counts the values received.
A call with no arguments is valid. The list is then empty.

notes.text: A call with no arguments is fine.

exercises.title: Variadic and loop
exercises.guide: Make the parameter variadic, and walk over the values it received.

exercises.title: A fixed parameter first
exercises.guide: Print a title, then each name that follows it.

chunks.guide: The variadic parameter goes last. Whatever comes before it is a normal parameter, filled first.

notes.text: Takes every argument after the title.

chunks.guide: The first argument is the title. All the rest become `names`.

exercises.title: What does it print?
exercises.guide: Read the code, then pick the output.
exercises.explanation: In the first call `extra` is 10 and `nums` holds 1 and 2, so it returns 13. In the second `nums` is empty, so the loop never runs and `extra` comes back as 10.

slides.text: Sometimes the values are already in a slice. You write one with its type and the values in braces. The type `[]int` means a slice of ints.
Passing the slice as one argument does not work: the function wants separate values. Put `...` after the slice and Go **spreads** it, so each value becomes its own argument.
Inside the function, the slice you spread and the parameter point at the same values. Keep that in mind when a function changes what it received.

exercises.title: Spread a slice
exercises.guide: Multiply any amount of numbers, then call it with a slice.

chunks.guide: The package and the import are already in the file. Start the result at 1, because multiplying by 0 would wipe it out.
`...` after the slice turns its values into separate arguments. Plain values still work.

notes.text: Passes each value as a separate argument.

exercises.title: Declare and spread
exercises.guide: Make the parameter variadic, and spread the slice in the call.

exercises.title: The same values
exercises.guide: Change the first value inside a function, and see the slice outside.

chunks.guide: `nums[0]` is the first value: positions start at 0. Assigning to it replaces that value.

notes.text: Replaces the first value of the list.

chunks.guide: Spreading hands the function your own slice, not a copy. Printing a slice shows its values in brackets.

exercises.title: First and last
exercises.guide: Return the first and the last value, whichever way they were passed.

chunks.guide: A variadic function can return several values. The last position is one less than the length.

notes.text: Positions start at 0, so the last is length minus 1.

chunks.guide: Receive both results, and print them.
Reuse the two variables with `=`, this time from a slice.

exercises.title: What does it print?
exercises.guide: Read the code, then pick the output.
exercises.explanation: With no arguments `nums` is empty, so the guard returns -1. With `7, 8` it returns the first value, 7.
